problems.title: Simulated annealing on a solar HALE wing skin layup
problems.setup: A solar HALE aircraft wing skin is a stack of composite plies, and each design is a discrete stacking sequence. The objective f is skin mass in kg after sizing for buckling. Simulated annealing proposes a neighbour by swapping two adjacent plies and accepts it with the Metropolis rule P = min(1, exp(−Δf/T)), where Δf = f_new − f_current and T is the temperature in kg. The current design has f = 41.2 kg and the proposed swap gives f = 41.8 kg. The run is at T = 1.0 kg.

parts.ask: Find the probability of accepting the proposed swap.
The random number drawn from U(0, 1) is r = 0.42. What does the algorithm do?
parts.a: Accept the heavier design, since r = 0.42 < P = 0.549
w: Reject it, since every uphill move is rejected
Reject it, since r = 0.42 < P means rejection
Accept it only if the move also lowers the best mass found so far
sol: Uphill acceptance lets the search climb out of a local basin
The best design found so far is stored separately

parts.ask: Restart tuning: choose the start temperature T₀ so that a typical uphill move of Δf = 0.6 kg is accepted with probability 0.8.
sol: A hot start accepts most moves and explores widely

parts.ask: Cool geometrically, T_k = T₀·0.85ᵏ. After how many cooling steps k does the acceptance probability for Δf = 0.6 kg first fall below 0.01?
At that cold temperature the next proposal gives Δf = −0.3 kg. What is its acceptance probability?
parts.a: 1: every downhill move is accepted at any temperature
w: exp(−0.3/T), about 0.1 at T = 0.13 kg
exp(0.3/T) capped at 0.5
0.01, the same as the uphill move at this temperature
sol: Cold SA behaves like a greedy descent on the neighbourhood

problems.x: Simulated annealing always accepts downhill moves and accepts an uphill move Δf with probability exp(−Δf/T), so a slowly falling temperature turns broad exploration into local refinement.

problems.title: Electric commuter: drag against trip time by ε-constraint
problems.setup: An electric commuter with W = 60000 N cruises a R = 300 km route at 3000 m (ρ = 0.9 kg/m³). Wing S = 30 m², AR = 10, e = 0.8, C_D0 = 0.025. Cruise drag sets battery energy per trip: D(V) = aV² + b/V² with a = ½ρSC_D0 and b = 2W²/(ρSπe·AR). The two objectives are drag D (energy) and trip time t = R/V, and the airline wants the Pareto front between them.

parts.ask: One end of the front is the minimum energy design. Find its cruise speed.
Which statement is the ε-constraint scalarization that traces the front?
parts.a: min over V of D(V) subject to R/V ≤ ε, solved for a sweep of trip time limits ε
w: min over V of wD(V) + (1 − w)R/V for a sweep of w, with ε as the step in w
min over V of R/V subject to D(V) = ε, solved once at the utopia point
min over V of D(V) + ε(R/V)², with ε driven to zero
sol: Keep one objective, turn the other into a constraint with bound ε
Each ε gives one Pareto point
The method reaches every Pareto point, including points in nonconvex parts of a front

parts.ask: The schedule requires ε = 50 min. Find the cruise drag on the front.
sol: V_md gives 66.8 min > 50 min, so the time constraint is active

parts.ask: With L = D + μ(R/V − ε), find the multiplier μ at ε = 50 min.
sol: μ = −dD/dε: each extra second of trip time saves 1.54 N of drag, the local slope of the front

parts.ask: What if the schedule relaxes to ε = 75 min? Find the cruise drag.
sol: At V_md the trip takes 66.8 min ≤ 75 min, so the constraint is inactive and μ = 0
Every ε beyond 66.8 min returns this same end point of the front

problems.x: The ε-constraint method minimizes one objective with the other bounded by ε, and its multiplier μ equals the local trade-off slope −dD/dε of the Pareto front.

problems.title: Sailplane twist by CFD: the exact trust region step
problems.setup: A sailplane wing twist distribution is tuned with two variables, root and tip twist increments p (degrees), and each drag evaluation is a costly CFD run (f in drag counts). At the current design the model is m(p) = f + gᵀp + ½pᵀBp with g = (−2.4, −8) counts/deg and B = diag(2, 8) counts/deg². The trust radius is Δ = 1 deg. Solve the subproblem exactly: min m(p) subject to ‖p‖ ≤ Δ. Radius rule: ρ < 0.25 shrink Δ to Δ/4 (reject if ρ ≤ 0); ρ > 0.75 with ‖p‖ = Δ double Δ; otherwise keep Δ.

parts.ask: Find the length of the full Newton step p_N = −B⁻¹g.
sol: The solution lies on the boundary ‖p‖ = Δ

parts.ask: Which conditions characterize the exact solution p* of the trust region subproblem?
parts.a: (B + λI)p* = −g, λ ≥ 0, λ(Δ − ‖p*‖) = 0, and B + λI positive semidefinite
w: (B − λI)p* = g, λ ≤ 0, and ‖p*‖ < Δ
Bp* = −g scaled down to length Δ, with λ = 0
(B + λI)p* = −g with λ chosen so that B + λI = I
sol: These are the KKT conditions of min m(p) s.t. ½‖p‖² ≤ ½Δ²
λ is the multiplier of the radius constraint
λ = 0 gives Newton inside the region, λ → ∞ turns p toward −g

parts.ask: Find λ such that ‖p(λ)‖ = Δ, where p(λ) = −(B + λI)⁻¹g.
sol: ‖p(λ)‖ falls monotonically with λ, so this root is unique

parts.ask: The CFD run at x + p* shows an actual drag reduction of 3.9 counts. Find ρ.
sol: ρ > 0.75 with ‖p‖ = Δ: accept and double Δ to 2 deg

parts.ask: What if the radius had been Δ = 2 deg? Find the predicted reduction of the exact step.

problems.x: The exact trust region step solves (B + λI)p = −g with λ ≥ 0 sized so the step fits the radius, and λ = 0 recovers the Newton step whenever it already lies inside.

problems.title: Is cruise drag convex in speed and wing area?
problems.setup: A small UAV with W = 2000 N flies level at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) with C_D0 = 0.02 and K = 0.04. Treat speed V and wing area S as design variables: D(V, S) = P + Q with parasite drag P = ½ρV²SC_D0 and induced drag Q = KW²/(½ρV²S). Second derivatives can be written with P and Q: D_VV = (2P + 6Q)/V², D_VS = (2P + 2Q)/(VS), D_SS = 2Q/S².

parts.ask: State the second-order test you will use for convexity.
parts.a: On a convex domain (here V > 0, S > 0), D is convex if and only if its Hessian is positive semidefinite at every point of the domain
w: D is convex if its Hessian is positive definite at the minimizer
D is convex if every diagonal entry of the Hessian is positive everywhere
D is convex if the Hessian determinant is positive at one interior point
sol: State the zeroth-order definition first: D(θx + (1 − θ)y) ≤ θD(x) + (1 − θ)D(y)
For twice differentiable D on a convex set, it is equivalent to ∇²D ⪰ 0 everywhere
Positive diagonals alone allow a negative determinant

parts.ask: Evaluate det ∇²D at V = 50 m/s, S = 4 m².
What does the sign of the determinant tell you about D(V, S)?
parts.a: det ∇²D has the sign of Q − P, so the Hessian is indefinite wherever parasite drag exceeds induced drag and D is nonconvex on V > 0, S > 0
w: The determinant is negative at one point only, so D is convex everywhere else and therefore convex
A negative determinant means the Hessian is negative definite, so D is concave
D is a sum of two convex terms in (V, S), so it is convex and the determinant was miscalculated
sol: At V = 30 m/s, S = 4 m²: P = 44.1 N < Q = 72.6 N and det = +1.50
One point with an indefinite Hessian is enough to break convexity
With a = ½ρC_D0, the term aV²S alone has Hessian [[2aS, 2aV],[2aV, 0]] with det −4a²V² < 0

parts.ask: Twist: substitute v = ln V and s = ln S, so D = αe^(2v + s) + βe^(−2v − s) with α = ½ρC_D0 and β = 2KW²/ρ. Find ∂²D/∂v² at the same point.
sol: D depends on u = 2v + s only, with d²D/du² = P + Q
∇²D in (v, s) = (P + Q)[[4, 2],[2, 1]], positive semidefinite everywhere
Sums of exponentials of affine functions are convex: this is the geometric programming transformation

parts.ask: Find the minimum drag over all (V, S).
sol: Minimum where P = Q, so D_min = 2√(PQ) = 2W√(KC_D0)
It holds along the whole curve V²S = const: a valley of minimizers, matching the singular log-space Hessian

problems.x: Convexity depends on the choice of variables: cruise drag is nonconvex in (V, S) where parasite drag dominates, and becomes convex in (ln V, ln S) as a geometric program.

problems.title: Titan rotorcraft blade section: a quadratic surface from four CFD runs
problems.setup: A Titan rotorcraft blade section is studied in coded thickness x₁ and camber x₂. Four CFD runs at the corners give profile drag y in counts: y(−1, −1) = 118, y(1, −1) = 130, y(−1, 1) = 104, y(1, 1) = 124. The surrogate is the full quadratic ŷ = w₀ + w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + w₁₁x₁² + w₁₂x₁x₂ + w₂₂x₂², linear in the parameters, with Φᵢⱼ = φⱼ(xᵢ).

parts.ask: Classify the fitting problem and give the matrix you must invert.
parts.a: m = 6 basis functions and n = 4 samples: underdetermined, so pick the minimum norm w = Φᵀ(ΦΦᵀ)⁻¹y with ΦΦᵀ of size 4 × 4
w: m = 6 and n = 4: solve the 6 × 6 normal equations ΦᵀΦw = Φᵀy directly
m = 4 and n = 6: overdetermined least squares with ΦᵀΦ of size 4 × 4
m = n = 4 after dropping x₁x₂: interpolate with w = Φ⁻¹y
sol: Φ is n × m = 4 × 6, rank 4, so ΦᵀΦ (6 × 6) is singular
Infinitely many w fit all four points exactly
min ‖w‖² s.t. Φw = y gives w = Φᵀa with (ΦΦᵀ)a = y

parts.ask: Use the summation form (ΦΦᵀ)ᵢₖ = Σⱼ φⱼ(xᵢ)φⱼ(xₖ) and wⱼ = Σᵢ aᵢφⱼ(xᵢ) to find the interaction weight w₁₂.
sol: At the corners x₁² = x₂² = 1, so (ΦΦᵀ)ᵢₖ = 3 + x₁ᵢx₁ₖ + x₂ᵢx₂ₖ + (x₁x₂)ᵢ(x₁x₂)ₖ
Also w₁ = 8 and w₂ = −5, the usual main effects

parts.ask: Predict the drag at the centre (0, 0) with this minimum norm surrogate.
sol: Columns 1, x₁² and x₂² are identical at the corners, so the minimum norm splits the mean 119 equally: w₀ = w₁₁ = w₂₂ = 119/3
ŷ(0, 0) = 39.7 counts, about a third of every sample: a flag that the design leaves curvature unidentified

parts.ask: Dimension check for ridge regularization with λ > 0. Which statement is correct?
parts.a: (ΦᵀΦ + λI)w = Φᵀy uses a 6 × 6 matrix, a = (ΦΦᵀ + λI)⁻¹y uses a 4 × 4 matrix, and w = Φᵀa gives the same w
w: (ΦᵀΦ + λI) is 4 × 4 and (ΦΦᵀ + λI) is 6 × 6, and the two give different w
Ridge needs n > m, so it applies only after two more CFD runs
λI must be 4 × 6 to match Φ, so λ adds to every entry of Φ
sol: Push through identity: (ΦᵀΦ + λI)⁻¹Φᵀ = Φᵀ(ΦΦᵀ + λI)⁻¹
With λ = 2: w₁ = 8·4/6 = 5.33, shrunk toward zero

parts.ask: What if a fifth run at the centre gives y(0, 0) = 112? Find w₁₁ of the new minimum norm fit.
sol: Centre run: w₀ = 112; corners: w₀ + w₁₁ + w₂₂ = 119, so w₁₁ + w₂₂ = 7
Minimum norm splits it: w₁₁ = w₂₂ = 3.5
Axial points (±α, 0), (0, ±α) of a central composite design separate w₁₁ from w₂₂

problems.x: With fewer samples than basis functions the minimum norm weights w = Φᵀ(ΦΦᵀ)⁻¹y fit every sample, and the sample design decides which terms the data identify.

problems.title: Wing sizing by SQP: lift as an equality, a C_L cap and an active set QP
problems.setup: Size the wing of a UAV at fixed cruise q = 1000 Pa and W = 10000 N with variables x = (S, C_L). Minimize drag f = qS(C_D0 + KC_L²) with C_D0 = 0.02 and K = 0.05, subject to lift equals weight, h = qSC_L − W = 0, and a gust margin cap g = C_L − 0.5 ≤ 0. Use L = f + λh + μg. Start SQP at x₀ = (25 m², 0.4) with λ₀ = −0.07 N/N, which gives the Lagrangian Hessian H_L = [[0, −30],[−30, 2500]]. The QP is min ∇fᵀp + ½pᵀH_Lp subject to h + ∇hᵀp = 0 and g + ∇gᵀp ≤ 0.

parts.ask: Why is lift written as an equality constraint here instead of being substituted?
parts.a: Keeping S and C_L as independent variables with h = qSC_L − W = 0 lets the optimizer see the lift requirement, and its multiplier λ prices one newton of extra weight in drag
w: Lift is an inequality qSC_L ≥ W, so it can be dropped when C_L is capped
Lift belongs in the objective as a penalty (qSC_L − W)², with no multiplier
Lift equals weight automatically at the drag minimum, so h is redundant
sol: Substituting C_L = W/(qS) removes a variable, which works for one closed form polar
With many variables and a CFD polar, C_L = C_L,required is posed as an equality
At x₀: h = 1000·25·0.4 − 10000 = 0, so x₀ is lift feasible

parts.ask: First QP pass with working set {h} only. Find the C_L step p₂.
That step gives C_L = 0.52, which violates the linearized cap, so g joins the working set. Find the new wing area S₁ = S₀ + p₁.
sol: True lift at (18.75, 0.5) is 9375 N: h = −625 N from the bilinear term qp₁p₂, fixed by later iterations (optimum S = 20 m²)

parts.ask: Find the QP multiplier μ of the cap and decide whether g stays in the working set.
sol: μ > 0 and the step is feasible: the active set QP stops with g active

parts.ask: Twist: the drag polar is replaced by a CFD solver with state vector u and residuals R(x, u) = 0. In a full space (all at once) SQP, how do the flow equations enter?
parts.a: As equality constraints R(x, u) = 0 with u added to the optimization variables, linearized in each QP along with lift
w: As inequality constraints R(x, u) ≤ 0, since residuals only need to be small
As a term ‖R(x, u)‖² added to the drag objective
Only after convergence, as a final check on the optimum
sol: Full space: variables (x, u), constraints R = 0 and h = 0, the flow converges together with the optimum
Reduced space: solve R(x, u) = 0 inside every evaluation and use adjoint gradients
Either way lift appears as an equality constraint

problems.x: Design optimization poses lift and the governing equations R(x, u) = 0 as equality constraints, and SQP solves each QP by an active set loop that adds violated constraints and keeps those with μ ≥ 0.
